prompt.context: Our client, FC Limited (Fine China Limited) manufactures sets of fine china (plates, tea cups, etc). They only sell the china in sets (never as individual pieces) at $1,500 per set. Excess or lack of demand has never been a problem for FC, and they sell 10,000 sets per year. The company was started 50 years ago and has been successful and profitable throughout its history. However, in the last 7 years a key competitor recently entered the industry. FC has recently learned that the competitor has at least 50% higher margins and would like to match or exceed its results.
prompt.question: Why are FC's profit margins not as good as those of the new entrant? How do you propose FC fix this problem? Then, given the recommended changes, what does the new cost structure and profit margin look like?

clarifying_info.a: No. FC sells 10,000 sets per year, exactly meeting demand, and that number is not expected to change.

clarifying_info.q: How do FC's raw material costs compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Raw material costs (porcelain clay) are in-line with or less than those of competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How does FC's manufacturing compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Manufacturing takes place at FC's North Carolina headquarters and is efficient; costs are slightly lower than competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What does FC's distribution network look like?
clarifying_info.a: FC has 6 warehouses: 2 in North Carolina, 2 in Ohio, and 2 in Southern California. China is manufactured in North Carolina, then shipped to regional warehouses for quicker delivery to retailers when orders are placed.

clarifying_info.q: How is the china sold / what are the sales channels?
clarifying_info.a: China is sold exclusively as a set through upscale retail stores like Neiman Marcus and Saks Fifth Avenue. Retail stores do not hold inventory — they keep one display set and take orders for next-day pick-up or occasional personal home delivery.
White-glove service is required — no damage or sloppiness permitted. This is why the warehouse network exists.

clarifying_info.q: How does FC ship the china to warehouses?
clarifying_info.a: When the company started they used railroads; in the last 30 years they moved to trucks.

clarifying_info.q: What does the key competitor's distribution look like?
clarifying_info.a: The competitor is located in Tennessee (Memphis). They have one warehouse and use FedEx from their manufacturing site to ship directly to retailers, also meeting a one-day delivery commitment.

clarifying_info.q: How does pricing compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: FC's pricing is in-line with or slightly higher than competitors. Pricing will not change.

clarifying_info.q: How much does white-glove common-carrier shipping cost?
What is a good proxy for evaluating the fixed cost mix?
clarifying_info.a: Square footage in facilities. The factory is twice the size of the average warehouse.

exhibits.title: Fine China, Ltd. — Income Statement (Interviewer Only)
exhibits.shows: A two-column income statement table comparing the current cost structure and a proposed new cost structure. Rows include Revenue, and five cost line items: Raw Materials, Fixed Overhead, Labor, Shipping, and Inventory Costs. Each cost item shows its percentage of total costs and dollar amounts. The table also shows Total Costs and Profit Margin for both scenarios.
exhibits.data: Revenue: $15,000,000 (both scenarios); Total current costs: $12,000,000 (given); Cost breakdown as % of $12mm: Raw Materials 20%, Fixed Overhead 40%, Labor 20%, Shipping 10%, Inventory Costs 10%; Current profit margin: 20%

framework: Diagnose whether the margin gap is a revenue problem or a cost problem (revenue is confirmed stable — focus on costs)
Map the full value chain: raw materials → manufacturing → distribution/warehousing → shipping → retail
Compare each value-chain node to the competitor: raw materials (in-line), manufacturing (slightly better), distribution/warehousing (key gap), shipping method (key gap)
Identify root cause: FC operates 6 regional warehouses + truck shipping vs. competitor's 1 warehouse + FedEx direct-to-retailer
Recommend eliminating most warehouse space and switching to overnight carrier (FedEx/UPS) for direct-to-retailer fulfillment
Quantify the cost impact: model new income statement and calculate new profit margin

questions.prompt: Question 1: Why are FC's profit margins lower than the competitor's, and how should FC fix this?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates quickly reframe this as a supply chain case, not just a profitability case. They map the value chain, rule out revenue and upstream cost issues (raw materials and manufacturing are fine), and zero in on the distribution network. FC's 6-warehouse + truck model was built in an era before overnight shipping; the competitor uses a single hub + FedEx to achieve the same 1-day delivery promise at lower cost. Recommendation: eliminate most warehouse space and shift to overnight carrier direct shipping to retailers.

questions.prompt: Question 2a: What does the current income statement and cost structure look like? Calculate current revenue and profit margin.
questions.guidance: The candidate should derive the income statement interactively. The interviewer gives total costs of $12mm and reveals each cost line's % of total as the candidate names the categories. The candidate must also calculate revenue independently. Key insight: Fixed Overhead (warehousing) is the single largest cost at 40% of total, consistent with the diagnosis in Q1.

math.setup: Revenue = sets sold × price per set; Profit = Revenue − Total Costs; Margin = Profit / Revenue
steps: Cost breakdown (% of $12mm): Raw Materials 20% = $2,400,000; Fixed Overhead 40% = $4,800,000; Labor 20% = $2,400,000; Shipping 10% = $1,200,000; Inventory Costs 10% = $1,200,000
math.answer: Current profit margin is 20%; revenue is $15,000,000; total costs are $12,000,000.

questions.prompt: Question 2b: Given FC eliminates most warehouse space, what cost reductions can be achieved and what is the new profit margin?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify each reducible cost head and explain the intuition behind the reduction. The interviewer then confirms the expected % reduction for each. Fixed Overhead drops most (50%) because most warehouses are eliminated but one NC location is kept. Labor drops 25% from fewer loading/unloading staff. Shipping increases 25% because FedEx is more expensive per shipment than trucking. Inventory Costs drop 50% because less stock sits in warehouses. Raw Materials are unchanged (same production volume). The candidate should compute new total costs, profit, and margin — approximately 42%.

math.setup: New cost per line = Old cost × (1 + % change); New Total Costs = sum of new line costs; New Profit = Revenue − New Total Costs; New Margin = New Profit / Revenue
steps: Raw Materials: $2,400,000 × (1 − 0%) = $2,400,000 (no change; same production volume)
Fixed Overhead: $4,800,000 × (1 − 50%) = $2,400,000 (reduction of $2,400,000; most warehouses eliminated, one NC site kept)
Labor: $2,400,000 × (1 − 25%) = $1,800,000 (reduction of $600,000; fewer workers loading/unloading at warehouses)
Shipping: $1,200,000 × (1 + 25%) = $1,500,000 (increase of $300,000; FedEx more expensive than trucking overall)
Inventory Costs: $1,200,000 × (1 − 50%) = $600,000 (reduction of $600,000; less inventory held in warehouses)
math.answer: New profit margin is approximately 42%, up from 20% — more than doubling profitability.

recommendation: FC should eliminate most of its 6 regional warehouses (retaining minimal space in North Carolina near the factory) and shift from truck-based regional distribution to overnight carrier service (FedEx or UPS) for direct-to-retailer shipment.

This mirrors the competitor's model and allows FC to maintain its one-day delivery commitment with a white-glove service at a cost of approximately $150 per set, which is more than offset by the savings in fixed overhead, labor, and inventory costs.
risks: White-glove common-carrier shipping is more expensive per shipment; if volumes increase sharply the shipping cost line will grow.
Transition risk: closing warehouses and retraining logistics operations may cause temporary service disruptions.
FC retains some fixed overhead in North Carolina; if the NC facility is also over-sized relative to need, further optimization may be warranted.
next_steps: Negotiate a volume contract with FedEx or UPS for white-glove service at a competitive rate.
Develop a warehouse wind-down plan, including disposition of leases and redeployment or severance of warehouse staff.
Monitor shipping costs and delivery performance post-transition to ensure the one-day commitment is maintained.
Evaluate whether any portion of the NC warehouse space can be sub-let or repurposed to further reduce fixed overhead.
